summary: Describes how to carry label mapping information for a route inside the same BGP Update message that announces the route. This lets routers distribute labels, such as those used in label-switched forwarding, together with routing information. It was replaced by RFC 8277.

plainLanguage.summary: Some networks forward traffic using short labels instead of looking up an address in a routing table at every hop. This RFC says how a BGP router can hand out those labels in the very same message where it announces the route they belong to, so no second protocol is needed to spread the labels.

questions: how to carry mpls labels in bgp
how does bgp carry mpls labels
subtitle: How BGP routers hand out MPLS labels in the same update message that announces the route.

tldr.problem: Routers that exchange routes with BGP also need to exchange the MPLS labels for those routes, and running a separate label distribution protocol for that is extra work.
tldr.mechanism: The label travels in the same BGP Update message as the route, inside the network reachability information of the Multiprotocol Extensions attribute, and SAFI value 4 marks that a label is present.
tldr.outcome: Labels can ride along with routes, including through Route Reflectors. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 8277 and updated by RFC 6790.

facts.label: Label field size
facts.value: 3 octets: 20 bits of value plus 1 bottom-of-stack bit

today: RFC 3107 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8277 and updated by RFC 6790, so read those for the current rules.

sections.title: Labels Piggybacked on Routes
sections.content:
When BGP distributes a route, it can also distribute an MPLS label mapped to that route. This RFC specifies how: the label mapping information for a route is piggybacked in the same BGP Update message used to distribute the route itself.

The RFC names three situations where this helps. Two adjacent Label Switched Routers (LSRs) that are also BGP peers can distribute labels with no other label distribution protocol at all. In a network split into exterior LSRs, which interface to other networks, and interior LSRs, which only carry traffic between the exterior LSRs, the interior routers need not receive any BGP routes at all as long as they support MPLS. And when BGP speakers exchange routes through a Route Reflector, the Route Reflector can distribute the labels as well, which the RFC says improves scalability quite significantly.

A BGP speaker may not use BGP to send labels to a particular peer unless that peer has said, through BGP Capability Advertisement, that it can process Update messages with the given SAFI.
sections.plainLanguage: One BGP message carries two things: the route to a destination and the label that belongs to it. That removes the need to run a second protocol just to hand out labels.

sections.title: Carrying Label Mapping Information
sections.content:
Label mapping information is carried as part of the Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) in the Multiprotocol Extensions attributes. The AFI indicates, as usual, the address family of the associated route, and SAFI value 4 indicates that the NLRI contains a label.

The NLRI is encoded as one or more triples of the form <length, label, prefix>:

  • Length is one octet and gives the length in bits of the address prefix plus the label or labels.
  • Label carries one or more labels, matching the stack of labels. Each label is encoded as 3 octets: the high-order 20 bits hold the label value and the low-order bit holds the Bottom of Stack flag.
  • Prefix contains the address prefix followed by enough trailing bits to end the field on an octet boundary. The value of those trailing bits is irrelevant.

The labels for a route must be assigned by the LSR identified by the value of the Next Hop attribute of the route. A BGP speaker that redistributes a route must not change its labels, except by omitting them, unless it also changes the Next Hop attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry in the route list has three parts: a length, a label and an address prefix. The label is three bytes long. Twenty bits carry the label number and one bit says whether more labels are stacked underneath it.

sections.title: Withdrawing Routes and Advertising Several
sections.content:
A BGP speaker can withdraw a previously advertised route, and the binding between that route and its label, in either of two ways: by advertising a new route and label with the same NLRI as before, or by listing the old NLRI in the Withdrawn Routes field of an Update. The label information carried in the Withdrawn Routes field should be set to 0x800000. Terminating the BGP session also withdraws every previously advertised route.

A BGP speaker may maintain and advertise more than one route to a given destination, as long as each such route has its own labels. The encoding above allows a single BGP Update message to carry several such routes, each with its own labels.

When a route is withdrawn and a label is given at the time of withdrawal, only the route with that label is withdrawn. When a route is withdrawn with no label given, only the corresponding unlabeled route is withdrawn and the labeled routes are left in place.
sections.plainLanguage: To take a route back, a router either announces the same route again with a new label, or sends a separate withdrawal message. If the withdrawal names a label, only that one route goes away.

sections.title: Capability Advertisement
sections.content:
A BGP speaker that uses Multiprotocol Extensions to carry label mapping information should use the Capabilities Optional Parameter to inform its peers about this capability. The MP_EXT Capability Code, as defined in the Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4 document, is used to advertise the (AFI, SAFI) pairs available on a particular connection.

A BGP speaker should not advertise this capability to another BGP speaker unless there is a Label Switched Path (LSP) between the two speakers. A speaker that is capable of handling multiple routes to a destination should also use the Capabilities Optional Parameter to inform its peers about that capability. The value of this capability is 4.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending labels, a router tells its neighbours it can handle them, using the optional parameters that BGP carries during connection setup. It should only do this if a label-switched path already exists between the two routers.

sections.title: When the BGP Peers Are Not Adjacent
sections.content:
Consider the LSR topology A--B--C--D. Suppose that D distributes a label L to A. In this topology, A cannot simply push L onto a packet's label stack and send the resulting packet to B. D must be the only LSR that sees L at the top of the stack. Before A sends the packet to B, it must push on another label, which was distributed by B. B must replace this label with yet another label, which was distributed by C. In other words, there must be an LSP between A and D. If there is no such LSP, A cannot make use of label L. This is true any time labels are distributed between non-adjacent LSRs, whether that distribution is done by BGP or by some other method.

This document does not specify any procedure for ensuring in real time that label distribution between non-adjacent LSRs is done only when the appropriate MPLS infrastructure exists in the network or networks connecting the two LSRs. Ensuring that the proper infrastructure exists is an issue for network management and operation.
sections.plainLanguage: If a router four hops away hands out a label, the routers in between must each have their own label for the same path. Each router swaps its own label for the next one as the packet passes, so only the router at the far end sees the original label.

sections.title: Label Spoofing
sections.content:
When an LSR A is directly connected to an LSR B over a point-to-point interface, A knows that packets arriving on that interface came from B. A can therefore discard any packet from B whose top label is not among the labels A distributed to B. This prevents label spoofing, the situation in which an LSR imposes a label that was never properly distributed to it.

These procedures are commonly used when the label distribution peers are separated not merely by a point-to-point link but by an MPLS network. Then A has no way to determine which other LSR pushed the top label, so it cannot tell whether that LSR was entitled to use it. When Route Reflectors are in use, A may not even know the set of LSRs which receive its label mappings.

Other techniques are possible. If labeled packets are never accepted from the network's external interfaces, and all the BGP-distributed labels are advertised via IBGP, there is no way for an untrusted router to put a labeled packet into the network. The condition can be weakened: it is enough to make sure that any labeled packet received on an external interface has a top label which was actually distributed out that interface.
sections.plainLanguage: On a direct link, a router knows which neighbour sent a packet, so it can check the label against the ones it handed out. Across an MPLS network that check is not possible, so the RFC suggests only accepting labeled packets from interfaces where the labels were actually distributed.
